claim: The study analyzed 2898 scientific papers published between 1995 and 2017 in which two or more authors shared the first author position.
source: We analyzed 2898 scientific papers published between 1995 and 2017 in which two or more authors shared the first author position.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and represents the dataset size and timeframe of the study.

claim: For papers in which the first and second authors made equal contributions, mixed-gender combinations were most frequent, followed by male-male and then female-female author combinations.
source: For papers in which the first and second authors made equal contributions, mixed-gender combinations were most frequent, followed by male-male and then female-female author combinations.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Table 1 and the Results section.

claim: For mixed-gender combinations, more male authors were in the first position, although the disparity decreased over time.
source: For mixed-gender combinations, more male authors were in the first position, although the disparity decreased over time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis showing temporal trends in the Results section.

claim: For papers in which three or more authors made equal contributions, there were more male authors than female authors in the first position.
source: For papers in which three or more authors made equal contributions, there were more male authors than female authors in the first position and more all-male than all-female author combinations.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in the Results section.

claim: There were more all-male than all-female author combinations for papers with three or more equal contributors.
source: For papers in which three or more authors made equal contributions, there were more male authors than female authors in the first position and more all-male than all-female author combinations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing 116 all-male vs 27 all-female combinations in Table 1.

claim: The gender inequalities observed among authors who made equal contributions are not consistent with random or alphabetical ordering of authors.
source: The gender inequalities observed among authors who made equal contributions are not consistent with random or alphabetical ordering of authors.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the Results section.

claim: The number of authors per publication has increased steadily in recent decades.
source: In recent decades, the number of authors per publication has increased steadily (National Library of Medicine, 2018; Colledge et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increase in authors per publication is caused by higher production of scientific information by research teams.
source: The causes for this trend include the higher production of scientific information by research teams (Wuchty et al., 2007) and an increase in the data content of published papers (Cordero et al., 2016; Fontanarosa et al., 2017), which in turn usually requires contributions by additional scientists.
evidence: This causal relationship is stated and supported by citations.

claim: Papers listing equal contributions comprised less than 1% of publications in 2000.
source: Papers listing equal contributions comprised less than 1% of publications in 2000, but by 2009 this figure had increased to between 1.0% and 8.6%, depending on the journal (Akhabue and Lautenbach, 2010).
evidence: This is a specific data point cited from a previous study.

claim: By 2009, papers listing equal contributions had increased to between 1.0% and 8.6%, depending on the journal.
source: Papers listing equal contributions comprised less than 1% of publications in 2000, but by 2009 this figure had increased to between 1.0% and 8.6%, depending on the journal (Akhabue and Lautenbach, 2010).
evidence: This is a specific data point cited from a previous study.

claim: For the journal Gastroenterology, 21% of papers published in 2011 and 2012 indicated two or more authors contributing equally.
source: For the journal Gastroenterology, for example, 21% of the papers published in 2011 and 2012 indicated two or more authors contributing equally (Dubnansky and Omary, 2012).
evidence: This is a specific data point cited from a previous study.

claim: Women are underrepresented in academic faculty and scientific positions, especially at senior ranks.
source: Numerous studies have documented underrepresentation of women in academic faculty and in scientific positions, especially at the more senior ranks (Awad et al., 2017; Sassler et al., 2017; John et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Women are less likely to occupy the first author position in scientific publications.
source: Several studies have documented gender differences in the frequency of first authors, with women less likely to occupy the first position (Fishman et al., 2017; Bonham and Stefan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Women are more likely to be middle authors and less likely to be senior authors in Swedish scientific publications.
source: A large study of Swedish scientists revealed that women are more likely to be middle authors and less likely to be senior authors (van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Two authors were listed as contributing equally in 2406 (83%) publications.
source: Two authors were listed as contributing equally in 2406 (83%) publications, while 492 (17%) listed three or more (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's dataset, also shown in Table 1.

claim: 492 (17%) publications listed three or more authors as contributing equally.
source: Two authors were listed as contributing equally in 2406 (83%) publications, while 492 (17%) listed three or more (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's dataset, also shown in Table 1.

claim: Of 972 mixed-gender two-author papers, 548 (56.38%) had the male author listed first and 424 (43.62%) had the female author listed first.
source: Of these, 1377 papers had two authors of the same gender (mm or ff), leaving 972 with mixed gender authors claiming equal contribution, which consisted of 548 (56.38%) where the male author was listed first and 424 (43.62%) where the female author was listed first.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The Chi-square statistic comparing expected and observed gender ratios for mixed-gender two-author papers was 15.8 (df = 1 and p<0.001).
source: Comparing the expected and observed gender ratios yielded a Chi-square statistic of 15.8 (df = 1 and p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: The difference between observed and expected gender ratios was significant in the 1996-2006 group (p<0.001).
source: When these ratios were analyzed with the Chi-square statistic the difference between observed and expected ratios was significant in the 1996–2006 group (p<0.001), but not in the 2007–2017 group (p=0.156).
evidence: This is a statistical result from temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The difference between observed and expected gender ratios was not significant in the 2007-2017 group (p=0.156).
source: When these ratios were analyzed with the Chi-square statistic the difference between observed and expected ratios was significant in the 1996–2006 group (p<0.001), but not in the 2007–2017 group (p=0.156).
evidence: This is a statistical result from temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The Odds Ratio of Gender Bias in First Authorship using year as a continuous variable was 0.958 (0.931–0.986), indicating an estimated 4.2% decrease in odds of preference for males in the first position per year.
source: The Odds Ratio of Gender Bias in First Authorship (95% Confidence Interval) using year as a continuous variable was 0.958 (0.931–0.986), indicating an estimated 4.2% decrease in odds of preference for males in the first position per year considering all publications from 1995 to 2017, adjusted for country, (95% CI: from 1% to 7% decrease per year, p-value=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the GEE analysis.

claim: The Odds Ratio comparing publications after 2007 to those in years 1995-2007 was 0.605 (0.443–0.828) with p=0.002.
source: The Odds Ratio comparing publications after 2007 to those in years 1995–2007 (95% confidence interval) using the year as a categorical variable and adjusting for country was 0.605 (0.443–0.828) with p=0.002.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the GEE analysis.

claim: Of 349 publications with three or more mixed-gender authors contributing equally, 201 (57.59%) listed a male author first while 148 (42.40%) listed a female author first.
source: Of these 349 publications, 201 (57.59%) listed a male author first while 148 (42.40%) listed a female author first.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: Comparing male author first versus female author first ratios for three or more authors yielded p=0.005.
source: Comparing male author first versus female author first ratios observed versus expected values yielded p=0.005.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: The frequency of publications with three or more authors contributing equally is increasing over time.
source: Analysis of the frequency of publications with three or more authors as a function of publication year revealed a positive trend line with time, suggesting that these author combinations are becoming more frequent (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3 showing a positive trendline.

claim: Overall, 49.6% of all publications had the authors names ordered alphabetically.
source: Overall, 49.6% of all publications had the authors names ordered alphabetically.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: Among publications where authors were ordered alphabetically, male-female author combinations were more common than female-male author combinations (Chi-square statistic is 4.359; p=0.037).
source: However, among those publications where the authors were ordered alphabetically male-female author combinations were more common than female-male author combinations (Chi-square statistic is 4.359; p=0.037).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: Male-male author combinations were the most common gender combination for both pairs and associations of more than two authors.
source: Male-male author combinations were the most common gender combination and this applied to combinations involving both pairs and association of more than two authors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Female-female author combinations comprised less than half the number of observed male-male author combinations.
source: Female-female author combinations were the least common gender combination comprising less than half the number of observed male-male author combinations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Table 1 showing 377 ff vs 1000 mm combinations.

claim: Male-female author combinations were significantly more frequent than female-male author combinations, with a ratio of 1.3:1.
source: Male-female author combinations were significantly more frequent than female-male author combinations, with a ratio of 1.3:1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and calculated from data showing 583 mf vs 446 fm combinations.

claim: The preference for males in the first author position among mixed-gender pairings was strongest for publications dating before 2007.
source: However, analysis of the data as a function of time revealed that the effect was strongest for publications dating before 2007.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by temporal statistical analysis.

claim: In the past decade, the preference for male gender in the first author position among mixed-gender pairings declined such that there was no statistical difference between observed gender order pairings and those expected from random assignments.
source: In the past decade, the preference for male gender in the first author position among mixed-gender pairings declined such that there was no statistical difference between observed gender order pairings and those expected from random assignments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the p=0.156 result for 2007-2017.

claim: The preference for males in the first author position occurred with author combinations of three or more authors listed as contributing equally, with a ratio of 1.35:1.
source: As with single pairings, the preference for males in the first author position also occurred with author combinations of three or more authors listed as contributing equally, with a ratio of 1.35:1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and calculated from data showing 201 male-first vs 148 female-first.

claim: There were almost four times more male only combinations than female only combinations when three or more authors contributed equally.
source: Male only combinations were also more common when three or more authors contributed equally such that there were almost four times more male only combinations than female only combinations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data showing 116 all-male vs 27 all-female combinations.

claim: In the biological sciences, the first author position is the person who is the most important contributor to the study.
source: In the biological sciences, the first author position is the person who is the most important contributor to the study and these are often students and postdoctoral fellows who are considered trainees.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about authorship conventions in biological sciences.

claim: First authors in biological sciences are often students and postdoctoral fellows who are considered trainees.
source: In the biological sciences, the first author position is the person who is the most important contributor to the study and these are often students and postdoctoral fellows who are considered trainees.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about authorship conventions in biological sciences.

claim: The proportion of women trainees in the biological sciences has exceeded that of men since 2000.
source: However, such an explanation would not apply for most papers published in the 21st century as the proportion of women trainees in the biological sciences, which this data set reflects, has exceeded that of men since 2000 (Committee on Women in Science, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a committee report.

claim: Information on equal contributions is often included as a footnote and for some publications is stated only in the pdf and print versions and are thus absent from the online full text versions.
source: We note that information on equal contributions is often included as a footnote and for some publications it is stated only in the pdf and print versions and are thus absent from the online full text versions, which are increasingly the format readers access.
evidence: This is an observation made during the study about publication practices.

claim: Male graduate students were 15% more likely to be listed in publications than their female counterparts.
source: A study of PhD students revealed that male graduate students were 15% more likely to be listed in publications than their female counterparts (Feldon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a large predominance of male authors over female authors in the first and last positions in natural sciences, social sciences, and the humanities.
source: An analysis of male and female authorship patterns for publications in natural sciences, social sciences, and the humanities showed that a large predominance of male author over female authors in the first and last positions (West et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Women receive less credit than men for team work in academia.
source: Perhaps most relevant for our findings is the observation that women receive less credit than men for team work in academia (Sarsons, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Males are more likely to share data with other men, which can lead to scientific discussions and collaborations that result in shared first author publications.
source: Nevertheless this observation is consistent with the finding that males are more likely to share data with other men, which can lead to scientific discussions and collaborations that result in shared first author publications (Massen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: At least two groupings of 11 authors claiming equal contribution were observed.
source: The frequency of multi-author equal contributions dropped rapidly for combinations of more than three authors, but we observed at least two groupings of 11 authors (Dastani et al., 2012; Ohlsson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study with citations to specific papers.

claim: None of the journal instructions for authors addressed equal contribution statements.
source: A recent analysis of journal instructions for authors revealed that none addressed equal contribution statements (Resnik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The patterns for Africa, Europe, and South America differed from the Asia, Australia, and North American groupings in author gender distribution.
source: We note with interest that the patterns for Africa, Europe, and South America differed from the Asia, Australia, and North American groupings, but caution against drawing conclusions since for some of these continent groupings the number of publications analyzed may not be adequate to make direct comparisons.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Female co-first authors were less represented in the first position in clinical journals compared to basic science journals.
source: In this regard, a recent study that examined papers published between 2005 and 2014 with co-first authors of different genders using online databases in addition to our method of website images, found that there was no difference in female versus male authors in the first position in basic science journals, which is consistent with our results, but that female co-first authors were less represented in the first position in clinical journals (Aakhus et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The study analyzed 3034 scientific publications from 1995 to 2017 where two or more authors stated to have contributed equally.
source: We analyzed 3034 scientific publications from 1995 to 2017 where two or more authors stated to have contributed equally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the initial dataset size.

claim: Gender was identified for each of the authors listed as contributing equally in 2898 publications.
source: From this set, we identified the gender for each of the authors listed as contributing equally in 2898 publications, which provided our usable dataset (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the usable dataset size.

claim: The study identified eight classes of author combinations claiming equal contribution.
source: We identified eight classes of author combinations claiming equal contribution: male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, more than two all-male, more than two all-female and more than two with mixed gender having either a male or female listed first (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The most common gender pairing for two equal contributors involved mixed gender.
source: For publications where two authors contributed equally, the most common gender pairing involved mixed gender, which was closely followed by male-male author pairings and female only author pairings were least frequent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The database of 2898 usable publications represents about 1.45% of the available publications with equal contributors in PubMed.
source: Hence, our database of 2898 usable publications represents about 1.45% of the available publications in this category.
evidence: This is calculated in the Materials and Methods section based on PubMed database size.

claim: Gender could not be reliably assigned to authors from name alone in approximately 4% of publications.
source: We could not reliably assign gender to authors from name alone in approximately 4% of publications.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section as a limitation of the study.

claim: Determination of author gender was done by searching for images of an individual's name using the Google search engine, which was adequate to assign gender for 97% of papers examined.
source: Determination of author gender was done by searching for images of an individual's name using the Google search engine, which was adequate to assign gender for 97% of papers examined.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section describing the methodology.

claim: The Google Scholar search strategy returned a higher frequency of male-female orderings among those sharing first position than the in-journal website search strategy.
source: Specifically, the Google Scholar search strategy was returning a higher frequency of male-female (M:F) orderings among those chairing first position than the in journal website search strategy.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section as an observation about search methodology.

claim: The Google Scholar search strategy was returning more older papers, suggesting a temporal variable to male-female author orderings.
source: Inspection of the identified articles revealed that that the Google Scholar search strategy was returning more older papers suggesting a temporal variable to male-female author orderings, a finding that was subsequently confirmed at the conclusion of the study.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section as an observation about search methodology.

claim: The analysis of each entry averaged approximately 5 minutes.
source: We estimate that the analysis of each entry averaged approximately 5 min, since each publication needed manual inspection to confirm that the search engine was correct and this often necessitated inspecting the PDF version of the publication, as author contributor information was not often available for the online format versions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section describing the time investment.

claim: Author contributor information was not often available for the online format versions of publications.
source: We estimate that the analysis of each entry averaged approximately 5 min, since each publication needed manual inspection to confirm that the search engine was correct and this often necessitated inspecting the PDF version of the publication, as author contributor information was not often available for the online format versions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and Methods section as an observation about publication formats.

claim: The disequilibrium in gender ratios among authors who contributed equally has abated in the past decade.
source: We note that the disequilibrium in gender ratios among authors who contributed equally has abated in the past decade.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by temporal statistical analysis.

claim: The effects of the disequilibrium measured in this study will linger for some time to come with disproportionately negative effects on women who shared first authorship and appeared second in the author byline.
source: Consequently, it is possible that the effects of the disequilibrium measured in this study will linger for some time to come with disproportionately negative effects on women who shared first authorship and appeared second in the author byline.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future consequences based on the study findings.

claim: A male preference in author ordering could have consequences on hiring decisions, promotion and the distribution of resources such as grant funding.
source: Given the importance of first authorship in biomedical publications and the increasing popularity of sharing authorship with the rise of team science a male preference could have consequences on hiring decisions, promotion and the distribution of resources such as grant funding.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences based on the study findings.

claim: Some authorship decisions are vulnerable to conscious or unconscious biases.
source: The finding of gender inequalities among authors who contributed equally raises the possibility that some authorship decisions are vulnerable to conscious or unconscious biases and this suggests the need for journals to require statements of how author ordering was done in publications claiming equal contributions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study findings about potential causes of observed inequalities.

claim: There is a need for journals to require statements of how author ordering was done in publications claiming equal contributions.
source: The finding of gender inequalities among authors who contributed equally raises the possibility that some authorship decisions are vulnerable to conscious or unconscious biases and this suggests the need for journals to require statements of how author ordering was done in publications claiming equal contributions.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The proportion of combinations in which a male author is listed first is decreasing over time.
source: The plot shows that the proportion of combinations in which a male author is listed first (various shades of blue) is decreasing over time.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown visually in the figure.

claim: The trendline R2 value for the percentage of papers with more than two authors claiming equal contribution is 0.4857.
source: Trendline R2 value as 0.4857.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 3.

claim: There were no differences in gender bias by country among papers with two equally contributing authors of different gender.
source: In these analyses, there were no differences in gender bias by country.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: The Generalized Linear Population-Average model showed a 1% decrease in odds of gender bias per year among publications with more than two equally contributing authors.
source: The results of the Generalized Linear Population-Average model described above showed a 1% decrease in odds of gender bias per year among publications with more than two equally contributing authors (estimated Odds Ratio = 0.99, 95% confidence interval: 0.933, 1.051).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the GEE analysis.

claim: Analysis of likelihood of male preference in the first author positions when three or more individuals contributed equally did not reveal any statistically significant associations with year of publication or country.
source: Analysis of likelihood of male preference in the first author positions when three or more individuals contributed equally did not reveal any statistically significant associations with year of publication or country.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: Among those publications where the authors were ordered alphabetically, there was no significant difference between the frequencies of alphabetical versus non-alphabetical ordering when comparing male vs. female author first position.
source: In comparing male vs, female author first position there was no significant difference between the frequencies of alphabetical versus no-alphabetical ordering.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 49% for male-male combinations.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 49% for male-female combinations.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 48% for female-male combinations.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 55% for female-female combinations.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 22% for three or more authors all male.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 41% for three or more authors all female.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 26% for three or more authors with male author first.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The percentage of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical was 25% for three or more authors with female author first.
source: The percentages of author associations for which the author sequence was alphabetical were 49%, 49%, 48%, 55%, 22%, 41%, 26%, and 25% for male-male, male-female, female-male, female-female, three or more authors all male, three or more authors all female, three or more authors male author first, and three or more authors female author first, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data point from the study's analysis.

claim: The author listed as contributing equally in the second position may not benefit as much as the author listed first.
source: Consequently, it is likely to that the author listed as contributing equally in the second position may be not benefit as much as the author listed first, which is usually recognized as the most important contributor in biomedical publications.
evidence: This is an inference based on publication practices and reader behavior.

claim: Some journals are encouraging citations to indicate both authors in equally contributed publications, instead of the traditional 'firstname et al.' format.
source: Recognizing this issue, some journals are encouraging citations to indicate both authors in equally contributed publications, instead of the traditional 'firstname et al.' format (Drubin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a journal editorial.

claim: The high prevalence of publications sharing first authorship among three or more males echoes the concern that male-exclusive networks exist in science.
source: The high prevalence of publications sharing first authorship among three or more males echoes the concern that male-exclusive networks exist in science (Massen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some have questioned whether statements of equal author contribution can ever be accurate given the problem of weighing the relative value of different contributions.
source: We note that some have questioned whether statements of equal author contribution can ever be accurate given the problem of weighing the relative value of different contributions (Moustafa, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous commentary.

claim: The majority of publications analyzed came from the United States.
source: The majority of publications analyzed came from the United States, reflecting the predominance of this country in contributing to the biomedical literature.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the data collected.

claim: The patterns of author combinations for Asia, Australia and North America were similar.
source: Analysis of distribution of author combinations for the continent of origin produced similar patterns for Asia, Australia and North America, which may reflect similar practices in author order selection in the contributing countries.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on data analysis.

claim: Similar patterns for Asia, Australia and North America may reflect similar practices in author order selection in the contributing countries.
source: Analysis of distribution of author combinations for the continent of origin produced similar patterns for Asia, Australia and North America, which may reflect similar practices in author order selection in the contributing countries.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed patterns.

claim: The finding that the preferences for males and females in the first author position varied over time suggests that variables contributing to these decisions may be changing rapidly.
source: The finding that the preferences for males and females in the first author position varied over time, suggests that variables contributing to these decisions may be changing rapidly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal trends observed in the data.

claim: There may be differences between fields that could skew results depending on the source database.
source: We noted differences between journals in the proportion of pairings, suggesting that that there may be differences between fields that could skew results depending on the source database.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and potential source of bias in the Discussion.

claim: The percentage of gender non-identification in this study (4%) compares favorably with the 5, 6 and 17% uncertainties reported in other studies using different methods.
source: We note that the percentage of gender non-identification in our study compares favorably with the 5, 6 and 17% uncertainties reported in other studies using different methods (van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2017; West et al., 2013; Bendels et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies supported by citations.

claim: Only 0.8% of all papers in PubMed have first authors that contribute equally.
source: However, given that only 0.8% of all papers in PubMed have first authors that contribute equally (Dubnansky and Omary, 2012), this would reduce the size of the database of interest to approximately 200,000 publications.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: At the beginning of this study, the Pubmed database had approximately 25,000,000 million entries.
source: At the beginning of this study, the Pubmed database had approximately 25,000,000 million entries.
evidence: This is stated as background information in the Materials and Methods section.

claim: Only one of the publications analyzed provided the rationale for the author order and indicated it was based on alphabetical ordering.
source: In fact, only one of the publications we analyzed provided the rationale for the author order and indicated it was based on alphabetical ordering (see, for example, Bieberstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study with citation to a specific paper.

claim: Having first author publications is a measure of success during the graduate and postdoctoral training years that can affect career trajectories.
source: Hence, having first author publications is measure of success during the graduate and postdoctoral training years that can affect career trajectories.
